content.narrative_summary: Section 2 outlines general principles for evaluating and managing valvular heart disease (VHD). In 2.1, the guideline recommends that all patients with known or suspected native VHD undergo thorough history‐taking and physical examination, electrocardiography, chest radiography, and comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography (2D and Doppler). Ancillary testing—such as transesophageal echocardiography, computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, stress testing, Holter monitoring, invasive hemodynamic assessment, or PET—may be needed to determine optimal treatment. Surgical or procedural risk estimation should consider comorbidities, frailty, and patient preferences. In 2.2, VHD severity classification is based on symptoms, valve anatomy, hemodynamics, ventricular/vascular function, and end‐organ effects; the progression of VHD is staged A through D, and indications for intervention or monitoring depend on symptom status, disease severity, ventricular response, and circulatory effects.

rows.recommendation: In patients with rheumatic heart disease, secondary prevention of rheumatic fever is indicated (Tables 6 and 7) (1).

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
content.narrative_summary: Recurrent rheumatic fever is associated with worsening rheumatic heart disease but can recur even when group A streptococcal infection is asymptomatic and treated. Tables 6 and 7 detail recommended antibiotic regimens and durations for secondary prophylaxis based on patient risk, valvular involvement, and age thresholds. For infective endocarditis prophylaxis, evidence from limited randomized and observational studies yields uncertainty: prophylactic antibiotics reduce bacteremia in high‐risk dental procedures but do not eliminate it, and data on procedural risk for nondental interventions are conflicting. The writing committee concludes prophylaxis is reasonable for highest‐risk patients undergoing qualifying dental procedures, with no benefit in nondental procedures absent active infection.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for IE Prophylaxis

rows.recommendation:
1. Antibiotic prophylaxis is reasonable before dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue, manipulation of the periapical region of teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa in patients with VHD who have any of the following (1–9):
a. Prosthetic cardiac valves, including transcatheter‐implanted prostheses and homografts.
b. Prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair, such as annuloplasty rings, chords, or clips.
c. Previous IE.
d. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or repaired congenital heart disease, with residual shunts or valvular regurgitation at the site of or adjacent to the site of a prosthetic patch or prosthetic device.
e. Cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation attributable to a structurally abnormal valve.

2. In patients with VHD who are at high risk of IE, antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for nondental procedures (eg, TEE, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, or cystoscopy) in the absence of active infection (10,11).

content.title: Recommendations for Anticoagulation for AF in Patients With VHD
section_headings: 2.4.3. Anticoagulation for AF in Patients With VHD
content.narrative_summary: The upper portion provides supportive text on infective endocarditis (IE) prophylaxis: IE risk is highest in patients with prosthetic valves, prior IE, or congenital heart disease with residual flow disturbances; TAVI-related IE rates match or exceed surgical AVR with high mortality; prosthetic material and transplant recipients have elevated IE risk; optimal oral hygiene and dental care reduce bacterial seeding; transient bacteremia from dental and gastrointestinal procedures is common but antibiotic prophylaxis lacks controlled evidence and may promote resistance. The bottom portion offers a synopsis of anticoagulation in valvular heart disease (VHD) with atrial fibrillation (AF): VKAs remain first choice for rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves, with NOACs as alternatives in select bioprosthetic and native VHD; supportive text regarding major RCTs comparing NOACs and warfarin begins but is incomplete.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Anticoagulation for AF in Patients With VHD

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with AF and native valve heart disease (except rheumatic mitral stenosis [MS]) or who received a bioprosthetic valve >3 months ago, a non-vitamin K oral anticoagulant (NOAC) is an effective alternative to VKA anticoagulation and should be administered on the basis of the patient’s CHA2DS2-VASc score (1,2).
2. For patients with AF and rheumatic MS, long-term VKA oral anticoagulation is recommended.
3. For patients with new-onset AF ≤3 months after surgical or transcatheter bioprosthetic valve replacement, anticoagulation with a VKA is reasonable (3–6).
4. In patients with mechanical heart valves with or without AF who require long-term anticoagulation with VKA to prevent valve thrombosis, NOACs are not recommended (7).

content.narrative_summary: This section discusses evidence regarding anticoagulation strategies in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and valvular heart disease (VHD). Meta-analyses, insurance-claims data, and large registries show no differential effect on thromboembolic outcomes between non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) and vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), with a net clinical benefit favoring NOACs in non-rheumatic VHD. Validation of the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score supports its use in VHD excluding moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS) and mechanical valves, and bioprosthetic valves are not independent predictors of thromboembolism. For new-onset postoperative AF after bioprosthetic valve implantation, data are conflicting, and VKAs are preferred in the first 3 months. The optimal duration of anticoagulation is undefined, and ongoing evaluation of rhythm and stroke risk is recommended.

content.title: 2.6. The Multidisciplinary Heart Valve Team and Heart Valve Centers
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes how multidisciplinary heart valve teams (MDTs) improve decision-making and optimize outcomes for patients with valvular heart disease by matching patients to providers with appropriate expertise and resources. Primary and Comprehensive Heart Valve Centers are defined by their procedural offerings and expertise in managing VHD. Recommendation-specific supportive text notes that MDTs are an established feature of heart valve programs and have been formally endorsed by the ACC, the American Society of Echocardiography, and other professional societies.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the Multidisciplinary Heart Valve Team and Heart Valve Centers

rows.recommendation: Patients with severe VHD should be evaluated by a Multidisciplinary Heart Valve Team (MDT) when intervention is considered.

Consultation with or referral to a Primary or Comprehensive Heart Valve Center is reasonable when treatment options are being discussed for 1) asymptomatic patients with severe VHD, 2) patients who may benefit from valve repair versus valve replacement, or 3) patients with multiple comorbidities for whom valve intervention is considered (1–19).

section_headings: 3.2.1.2. Diagnostic Testing: Changing Signs or Symptoms
content.narrative_summary: This page continues a discussion of noninvasive imaging and diagnostic approaches in aortic stenosis (AS), including use of CT for procedural planning, indications for repeat transthoracic echocardiography when physical examination or hemodynamic demands change (eg, surgery, pregnancy, infection, anemia), and the timing of routine follow-up in asymptomatic patients based on AS severity and comorbidities. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Exercise Testing in Patients With AS

rows.recommendation: In asymptomatic patients with severe AS (Stage C1), exercise testing is reasonable to assess physiological changes with exercise and to confirm the absence of symptoms (1–4).

In symptomatic patients with severe AS (Stage D1, aortic velocity ≥4.0 m/s or mean pressure gradient ≥40 mm Hg), exercise testing should not be performed because of the risk of severe hemodynamic compromise. (5)

content.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy of AS
content.narrative_summary: Under “Synopsis,” the guideline notes that medical treatment of hypertension and hyperlipidemia according to GDMT is appropriate for patients with AS, and ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy may reduce mortality in patients who have undergone TAVI. Recommendation‐specific supportive text states that hypertension is common in AS and may increase LV pressure overload; antihypertensive medications have not been shown to decrease cardiac output in AS; in the SEAS trial, hypertension was associated with higher rates of ischemic cardiovascular events and mortality; diuretics may reduce stroke volume when the LV chamber is small; ACE inhibitors may benefit LV fibrosis but optimal blood pressure targets in AS remain undefined; concurrent CAD is common and should be treated with GDMT and statin therapy for primary and secondary prevention.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy of AS

rows.recommendation: In patients at risk of developing AS (Stage A) and in patients with asymptomatic AS (Stages B and C), hypertension should be treated according to standard GDMT, started at a low dose, and gradually titrated upward as needed, with appropriate clinical monitoring (1–3).
In all patients with calcific AS, statin therapy is indicated for primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerosis on the basis of standard risk scores (4–6).
In patients who have undergone TAVI, renin–angiotensin system blocker therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARB) may be considered to reduce the long‐term risk of all‐cause mortality (7,8).
In patients with calcific AS (Stages B and C), statin therapy is not indicated for prevention of hemodynamic progression of AS (4–6).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Timing of Intervention of AS

rows.recommendation: In adults with severe high-gradient AS (Stage D1) and symptoms of exertional dyspnea, HF, angina, syncope, or presyncope by history or on exercise testing, AVR is indicated (1–7).
In asymptomatic patients with severe AS and an LVEF <50% (Stage C2), AVR is indicated (8–11).
In asymptomatic patients with severe AS (Stage C1) who are undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications, AVR is indicated (12–16).
In symptomatic patients with low-flow, low-gradient severe AS with reduced LVEF (Stage D2), AVR is recommended (17–24).
In symptomatic patients with low-flow, low-gradient severe AS with normal LVEF (Stage D3), AVR is recommended if AS is the most likely cause of symptoms (25–27).

In apparently asymptomatic patients with severe AS (Stage C1) and low surgical risk, AVR is reasonable when an exercise test demonstrates decreased exercise tolerance (normalized for age and sex) or a fall in systolic blood pressure of ≥10 mm Hg from baseline to peak exercise (13,28–30).
In asymptomatic patients with very severe AS (defined as an aortic velocity of ≥5 m/s) and low surgical risk, AVR is reasonable (15,31–35).
In apparently asymptomatic patients with severe AS (Stage C1) and low surgical risk, AVR is reasonable when the serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) level is >3 times normal (32,36–38).
In asymptomatic patients with high-gradient severe AS (Stage C1) and low surgical risk, AVR is reasonable when serial testing shows an increase in aortic velocity ≥0.3 m/s per year (39,40).
In asymptomatic patients with severe high-gradient AS (Stage C1) and a progressive decrease in LVEF on at least 3 serial imaging studies to <60%, AVR may be considered (8–11,33).
In patients with moderate AS (Stage B) who are undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications, AVR may be considered.

rows.recommendation: For symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with severe AS and any indication for AVR who are <65 years of age or have a life expectancy >20 years, SAVR is recommended (1–3).

For symptomatic patients with severe AS who are 65 to 80 years of age and have no anatomic contraindication to transfemoral TAVI, either SAVR or transfemoral TAVI is recommended after shared decision-making about the balance between expected patient longevity and valve durability (1,4–8).

For symptomatic patients with severe AS who are >80 years of age or for younger patients with a life expectancy <10 years and no anatomic contraindication to transfemoral TAVI, transfemoral TAVI is recommended in preference to SAVR (1,4–10).

In asymptomatic patients with severe AS and an LVEF <50% who are ≤80 years of age and have no anatomic contraindication to transfemoral TAVI, the decision between TAVI and SAVR should follow the same recommendations as for symptomatic patients in Recommendations 1, 2, and 3 above (1,2,4–10).

For asymptomatic patients with severe AS and an abnormal exercise test, very severe AS, rapid progression, or an elevated BNP (COR 2a indications for AVR), SAVR is recommended in preference to TAVI (1–3,11).

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), noting that TAVI is chosen via shared decision-making incorporating patient values. Clinical factors associated with poor TAVI outcomes include advanced age, frailty, pulmonary disease, hypertension, liver disease, stroke, anemia, and systemic conditions. The STS surgical risk score helps identify patients who benefit from TAVI; patients with mechanical impediments to surgical valve replacement may do better with TAVI, whereas those with a life expectancy <1 year or low likelihood of ‘survival with benefit’ are not recommended. Percutaneous aortic balloon dilation has limited long-term utility and modest symptomatic improvement, but carries risks and is not a substitute for surgical aortic valve replacement. The document then introduces acute aortic regurgitation (AR), describing its etiology—most commonly endocarditis, aortic dissection, or iatrogenic causes—and its hemodynamic consequences of severe volume overload and low forward output requiring urgent diagnosis and intervention. For diagnosis, transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography is indispensable to assess rapid aortic–left ventricular pressure equilibration, deceleration time, and half‐time of <300 ms; CT is the primary method to diagnose acute aortic dissection causing AR; MRI is rarely used acutely; TEE is useful intraoperatively and when CT is unavailable; sensitivities and specificities for Type A dissection by TTE and TEE are provided. Angiography is reserved for cases where noninvasive imaging is inconclusive or acute coronary syndrome is in the differential. In intervention, medical therapy to reduce left ventricular afterload may stabilize patients with severe AR due to endocarditis or dissection, but definitive surgery should not be delayed; intra‐aortic balloon counterpulsation is contraindicated; beta-blockers may be used cautiously, if at all, for other causes of acute AR.

content.title: 4.3.3. Timing of Intervention
content.narrative_summary: Initial synopsis states that vasodilating drugs do not reduce the severity of AR absent systemic hypertension and that GDMT for hypertension and HF applies to chronic asymptomatic AR similarly to the general population. A second paragraph notes that medical therapy is not a substitute for AVR in surgical candidates but can help alleviate symptoms in high–surgical-risk patients with comorbid conditions. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text explains that severe AR causes a wide pulse pressure, that heart-rate–lowering drugs may paradoxically increase blood pressure, and that ACE inhibitors or ARBs reduce systolic pressure without substantially lowering diastolic pressure. The final synopsis indicates that most patients with chronic severe AR require valve replacement, that valve-sparing may be possible in select anatomies though durability is unproven, and that AVR recommendations are based on measurements of LV dilation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Timing of Intervention for Chronic AR

rows.recommendation: 1. In symptomatic patients with severe AR (Stage D), aortic valve surgery is indicated regardless of LV systolic function (1–7).

2. In asymptomatic patients with chronic severe AR and LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF ≤55%) (Stage C2), aortic valve surgery is indicated if no other cause for systolic dysfunction is identified (3,5,8–12).
3. In patients with severe AR (Stage C or D) who are undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications, aortic valve surgery is indicated.

4. In asymptomatic patients with severe AR and normal LV systolic function (LVEF >55%), aortic valve surgery is reasonable when the LV is severely enlarged (LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m2) (Stage C2) (10,11,13–24).
5. In patients with moderate AR (Stage B) who are undergoing cardiac or aortic surgery for other indications, aortic valve surgery is reasonable.

6. In asymptomatic patients with severe AR and normal LV systolic function at rest (LVEF >55%; Stage C1) and low surgical risk, aortic valve surgery may be considered when there is a progressive decline in LVEF on at least 3 serial studies to the low-normal range (LVEF 55% to 60%) or a progressive increase in LV dilation into the severe range (LV end-diastolic dimension [LVEDD] >65 mm) (12,16,17,20,25–28).
7. In patients with isolated severe AR who have indications for SAVR and are candidates for surgery, TAVI should not be performed (29–32).

content.narrative_summary: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is a congenital anomaly affecting 0.5%–2.0% of adults with male predominance. Patients with BAV may develop isolated aortic valve disease (AS or AR) and frequently have aortopathy, with aneurysm formation in 20%–40%. Aortopathy involves dilation of the aortic sinuses, ascending aorta, or arch and occurs independently of valve function. Evaluation includes TTE for valve morphology, measurements of annulus, sinuses, sinotubular junction, and ascending aorta, and Doppler interrogation to assess coarctation. CT or CMR angiography is used when echocardiography is inadequate. Approximately 20%–30% of first-degree relatives of BAV patients may also have BAV or aortopathy; no specific genetic cause has been identified.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Initial Diagnosis of BAV

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with a known BAV, TTE is indicated to evaluate valve morphology, measure severity of AS and AR, assess the shape and diameter of the aortic sinuses and ascending aorta, and evaluate for the presence of aortic coarctation for prediction of clinical outcome and to determine timing of intervention (1–4).

2. In patients with BAV, CMR angiography or CT angiography is indicated when morphology of the aortic sinuses, sinotubular junction, or ascending aorta cannot be assessed accurately or fully by echocardiography. (4,5)

3. In first-degree relatives of patients with a known BAV, a screening TTE might be considered to look for the presence of a BAV or asymptomatic dilation of the aortic sinuses and ascending aorta. (6)

content.narrative_summary: This page presents Figure 5, a flowchart outlining imaging intervals for patients with bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), and a recommendation table for routine follow-up diagnostic testing in BAV patients, including Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Routine Follow-Up of Patients With a BAV

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with BAV and a diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta of ≥4.0 cm, lifelong serial evaluation of the size and morphology of the aortic sinuses and ascending aorta by echocardiography, CMR, or CT angiography is reasonable, with the examination interval determined by the degree and rate of progression of aortic dilation and by family history (1–5).
2. In patients with a BAV who have undergone AVR, continued lifelong serial interval imaging of the aorta is reasonable if the diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta is ≥4.0 cm (6,7).

rows.recommendation: In asymptomatic or symptomatic patients with a BAV and a diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta >5.5 cm, operative intervention to replace the aortic sinuses and/or the ascending aorta is recommended (1–3).

In asymptomatic patients with a BAV, a diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta of 5.0 to 5.5 cm, and an additional risk factor for dissection (eg, family history of aortic dissection, aortic growth rate >0.5 cm per year, aortic coarctation), operative intervention to replace the aortic sinuses and/or the ascending aorta is reasonable if the surgery is performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (3,4).

In patients with a BAV with indications for SAVR and a diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta ≥4.5 cm, replacement of the aortic sinuses and/or ascending aorta is reasonable if the surgery is performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (4–7).
In patients with a BAV who meet criteria for replacement of the aortic sinuses, valve‐sparing surgery may be considered if the surgery is performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (8,9).

In asymptomatic patients with a BAV who are at low surgical risk, have a diameter of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta of 5.0 to 5.5 cm, and have no additional risk factors for dissection, operative intervention to replace the aortic sinuses and/or the ascending aorta may be considered if the surgery is performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (4–7,10–14).

section_headings: 6.2.1. Diagnosis and Follow-Up of Rheumatic MS
content.narrative_summary: The narrative describes the pathologic features of mitral stenosis, noting fibrotic leaflet calcification, commissural fusion, and subvalvular involvement. It highlights that older patients often have additional comorbidities (atherosclerosis, hypertension, diastolic dysfunction). Nonrheumatic calcific MS is increasingly common in the elderly due to annular calcification extending into leaflets. Hemodynamic severity is best assessed by mitral valve area via 2D/3D planimetry or diastolic pressure half-time, although gradients depend on flow and heart rate. A valve area ≤1.5 cm2 defines severe MS, usually corresponding to a mean gradient >5 mm Hg. Alternative methods (continuity equation, Gorlin formula) may be used when discrepancies arise, particularly in rheumatic MS.

rows.recommendation: In patients with signs or symptoms of rheumatic MS, TTE is indicated to establish the diagnosis, quantify hemodynamic severity, assess concomitant valvular lesions, and demonstrate valve morphology (to determine suitability for mitral commissurotomy) (1–3).

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
section_headings: 6.2.1.2. Diagnostic Testing: Changing Signs or Symptoms
content.narrative_summary: For patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS), transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the initial imaging modality to assess stenosis severity and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC). When PMBC is being considered, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) evaluates concomitant mitral regurgitation (MR), left atrial (LA) anatomy, and excludes LA thrombus. TTE provides diastolic doming visualization, 3D area measurement, and Doppler gradients (with heart rate considerations), while TEE offers superior LA and mitral valve visualization in technically limited TTE studies and can detect LA appendage thrombi. Patients with changing symptoms—due to recurrent rheumatic fever, leaflet fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, or other valve lesions—should undergo repeat TTE to quantify mitral gradient and area. Rheumatic MS progresses slowly; routine follow-up TTE at intervals dictated by valve area is important even in asymptomatic patients. Cardiac catheterization, guided by TTE and sometimes TEE, is used when noninvasive findings are discordant or additional hemodynamic assessment is needed, measuring left ventricular (LV), LA, and pulmonary pressures and applying the Gorlin equation for valve area calculation.

content.title: 6.2.1.5 Diagnostic Testing: Exercise Testing
content.narrative_summary: Exercise testing with Doppler echocardiography or cardiac catheterization is useful when resting measurements do not align with clinical symptoms in patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis, with options including treadmill or bicycle exercise and hemodynamic assessment to quantify gradients and pulmonary pressures. In patients with rheumatic MS and atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation reduces thromboembolic risk, and heart rate control with beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, or ivabradine can improve diastolic filling and symptom management in those with tachycardia or rapid ventricular response.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Diagnostic Testing: Exercise Testing in Patients With Rheumatic MS

rows.recommendation: In patients with rheumatic MS and a discrepancy between resting echocardiographic findings and clinical symptoms, exercise testing with Doppler or invasive hemodynamic assessment is recommended to evaluate symptomatic response, exercise capacity, and the response of the mean mitral gradient and pulmonary artery pressure (1–5).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy in Patients With Rheumatic MS

rows.recommendation: In patients with rheumatic MS and 1) AF, 2) a prior embolic event, or 3) an LA thrombus, anticoagulation with a VKA is indicated (1–7).
In patients with rheumatic MS and AF with a rapid ventricular response, heart rate control can be beneficial (8).
In patients with rheumatic MS in normal sinus rhythm with symptomatic resting or exertional sinus tachycardia, heart rate control can be beneficial to manage symptoms (9–15).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for Rheumatic MS

rows.recommendation: In symptomatic patients (NYHA class II, III, or IV) with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm2, Stage D) and favorable valve morphology with less than moderate (2+) MR* in the absence of LA thrombus, PMBC is recommended if it can be performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center.

In severely symptomatic patients (NYHA class III or IV) with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm2, Stage D) who 1) are not candidates for PMBC, 2) have failed a previous PMBC, 3) require other cardiac procedures, or 4) do not have access to PMBC, mitral valve surgery (repair, commissurotomy, or valve replacement) is indicated.

In asymptomatic patients with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm2, Stage C) and favorable valve morphology with less than 2+ MR in the absence of LA thrombus who have elevated pulmonary pressures (pulmonary artery systolic pressure >50 mm Hg), PMBC is reasonable if it can be performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center.

In asymptomatic patients with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm2, Stage C) and favorable valve morphology with less than 2+/ MR* in the absence of LA thrombus who have new onset of AF, PMBC may be considered if it can be performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center.

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
section_headings: 7.2.2. Diagnosis and Follow-Up of Chronic Primary MR
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of management of acute severe mitral regurgitation (MR), noting that intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation and percutaneous circulatory assist devices can support systemic circulation before definitive therapy. Section 7.1.3 emphasizes that prompt mitral valve surgery, preferably repair, is lifesaving in symptomatic patients with acute severe primary MR, particularly in cases of papillary muscle rupture. Section 7.2 distinguishes chronic primary (degenerative) MR from chronic secondary (functional) MR. In chronic primary MR, pathology of the valve apparatus (leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, annulus) leads to regurgitation; myxomatous degeneration (Barlow’s valve), fibroelastic deficiency, and other etiologies (infective endocarditis, connective tissue disorders, rheumatic disease, radiation) are described. Prolonged volume overload causes myocardial damage, heart failure, and death, and correction before irreversible changes is curative. Section 7.2.2.1 introduces diagnostic testing for chronic primary MR.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Initial Diagnosis of Chronic MR

rows.recommendation: In patients with known or suspected primary MR, TTE is indicated for baseline evaluation of LV size and function, RV function, LA size, pulmonary artery pressure, and the mechanism and severity of primary MR (Stages A to D) (1–5).

In patients with primary MR, when TTE provides insufficient or discordant information, TEE is indicated for evaluation of the severity of MR, mechanism of MR, and status of LV function (Stages B to D).

In patients with primary MR, CMR is indicated to assess LV and RV volumes and function and may help with assessing MR severity when there is a discrepancy between the findings on clinical assessment and echocardiography (6–9).
In patients with severe primary MR undergoing mitral intervention, intraoperative TEE is indicated to establish the anatomic basis for primary MR (Stages C and D) and to guide repair (10,11).

content.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Routine Follow-Up for Chronic Primary MR
content.narrative_summary: The page provides two narrative synopses with supporting text. The first synopsis outlines that repeat transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is clinically relevant for patients with primary mitral regurgitation (MR) who develop new-onset symptoms and indicates mitral intervention criteria based on symptom onset and pathophysiological changes. The second synopsis addresses asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR, emphasizing periodic TTE surveillance of left ventricular (LV) function and pulmonary artery pressure, and discusses the potential adjunctive role of serum biomarkers and global longitudinal strain in guiding intervention timing.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Testing: Routine Follow-Up for Chronic Primary MR

rows.recommendation: For asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR (Stages B and C1), TTE is indicated every 6 to 12 months for surveillance of LV function (estimated by LVEF, LVEDD, and LVESD) and assessment of pulmonary artery pressure (1–11).

In asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR (Stages B and C1), use of serum biomarkers and novel measurements of LV function, such as global longitudinal strain, may be considered as an adjunct to guide timing of intervention (12–21).

content.narrative_summary: Left ventriculography and hemodynamic measurements are useful when noninvasive tests for MR severity, LV function, or surgical need are inconclusive, especially in symptomatic patients. Elevated filling pressures support a cardiac cause of dyspnea, while normal invasive hemodynamics in symptomatic patients may suggest noncardiac causes. Exercise echocardiography or invasive exercise hemodynamic testing can provide additional diagnostic and prognostic information in asymptomatic or symptomatic primary MR.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Diagnostic Testing: Exercise Testing for Chronic Primary MR

rows.recommendation: In patients with primary MR (Stages B and C) and symptoms that might be attributable to MR, hemodynamic exercise testing using Doppler echocardiography or cardiac catheterization or cardiopulmonary exercise testing is reasonable (1–4).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy for Chronic Primary MR

rows.recommendation: In symptomatic or asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR and LV systolic dysfunction (Stages C2 and D) in whom surgery is not possible or must be delayed, GDMT for systolic dysfunction is reasonable (1–3).
In asymptomatic patients with primary MR and normal LV systolic function (Stages B and C1), vasodilator therapy is not indicated if the patient is normotensive (4–8).

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: In patients with primary mitral regurgitation (MR), vasodilator therapy has not been shown to reduce MR severity; guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction or systemic hypertension should be implemented as in any patient with these conditions. Supportive text: Patients with MR and LV dysfunction experience myocardial damage and heart failure; when surgery is delayed or not performed, standard heart failure regimens—including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and possibly aldosterone antagonists—may help treat LV dysfunction alone. Data are sparse but favor beta-blockers in experimental MR. Vasodilator therapy shows limited or no durable benefit in chronic asymptomatic MR with normal LV function and may worsen MR unless used in acute severe symptomatic MR; hypertension must be treated to reduce morbidity and mortality.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for Chronic Primary MR

rows.recommendation: In symptomatic patients with severe primary MR (Stage D), mitral valve intervention is recommended irrespective of LV systolic function (1,2).
In asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR and LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF ≤60%, LVESD ≥40 mm) (Stage C2), mitral valve surgery is recommended (3–10).

In patients with severe primary MR for whom surgery is indicated, mitral valve repair is recommended in preference to mitral valve replacement when the anatomic cause of MR is degenerative disease, if a successful and durable repair is possible (11–15).

In asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR and normal LV systolic function (LVEF ≥60% and LVESD ≤40 mm) (Stage C1), mitral valve repair is reasonable when the likelihood of a successful and durable repair without residual MR is >95% with an expected mortality rate of <1%, when it can be performed at a Primary or Comprehensive Valve Center (4,13,16).

In asymptomatic patients with severe primary MR and normal LV systolic function (LVEF ≥60% and LVESD <40 mm) (Stage C1) but with a progressive increase in LV size or decrease in EF on ≥3 serial imaging studies, mitral valve surgery may be considered irrespective of the probability of a successful and durable repair (16).

In severely symptomatic patients (NYHA class III or IV) with primary severe MR and high or prohibitive surgical risk, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is reasonable if mitral valve anatomy is favorable for the repair procedure and patient life expectancy is at least 1 year (17,18).

content.narrative_summary:
The synopsis explains that anterior and bileaflet primary mitral regurgitation (MR) necessitates complex repair with less certain durability than simple posterior leaflet intervention; freedom from reoperation is ~80% and freedom from recurrent moderate or severe MR is ~60% at 15–20 years in complex cases. Outcomes are superior when repair is performed at high-volume centers, even in elderly patients, and repair should be attempted when feasible. Durable mechanical replacement may match repair outcomes in younger patients when managed with careful anticoagulation. Surgeon- and hospital-specific mitral volumes correlate with repair probability and outcomes; high-volume centers have ~50% lower mortality, though some low-volume centers also perform well. Volume metrics alone should not substitute for actual surgeon expertise. Combined severe MR and aortic stenosis is addressed elsewhere.

The recommendation-specific supportive text outlines: 1) primary MR is a mechanical leaflet coaptation problem requiring prompt surgical intervention upon symptom onset, 2) the therapeutic goal is correction before LV systolic dysfunction and adverse sequelae develop, 3) repair success improves with surgical volume and expertise, minimally invasive approaches may match full sternotomy outcomes when performed by experienced teams (operative mortality <1%, ~95% long-term survival, >80% freedom from reoperation at 15–20 years), and 4) onset of symptoms, LV dysfunction, or pulmonary hypertension worsens prognosis, so early mitral repair may obviate intensive surveillance and prevent negative sequelae (cut off mid-sentence).

rows.recommendation: 7. In symptomatic patients with severe primary MR attributable to rheumatic valve disease, mitral valve repair may be considered at a Comprehensive Valve Center by an experienced team when surgical treatment is indicated, if a durable and successful repair is likely (19).

8. In patients with severe primary MR where leaflet pathology is limited to less than one half the posterior leaflet, mitral valve replacement should not be performed unless mitral valve repair has been attempted at a Primary or Comprehensive Valve Center and was unsuccessful (11–14,20–22).

rows.recommendation: In patients with chronic secondary MR (Stages B to D), TTE is useful to establish the etiology and to assess the extent of regional and global LV remodeling and systolic dysfunction, severity of MR, and magnitude of pulmonary hypertension.

In patients with chronic secondary MR (Stages B to D), noninvasive imaging (stress nuclear/PET, CMR, or stress echocardiography), coronary CT angiography, or coronary arteriography is useful to establish etiology of MR and to assess myocardial viability.

In patients with chronic secondary MR with severe symptoms (Stage D) that are unresponsive to GDMT who are being considered for transcatheter mitral valve interventions, TEE is indicated to determine suitability for the procedure.
In patients with chronic secondary MR undergoing transcatheter mitral valve intervention, intra-procedural guidance with TEE is recommended.

rows.recommendation: Patients with chronic severe secondary MR (Stages C and D) and HF with reduced LVEF should receive standard GDMT for HF, including ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, aldosterone antagonists, and/or sacubitril/valsartan, and biventricular pacing as indicated (1–11).

In patients with chronic severe secondary MR and HF with reduced LVEF, a cardiologist expert in the management of patients with HF and LV systolic dysfunction should be the primary MDT member responsible for implementing and monitoring optimal GDMT (9,12).

content.title: Recommendations for Intervention for Secondary MR
content.narrative_summary: This section notes that secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) often responds to guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), including revascularization or cardiac resynchronization, under cardiologist supervision, and that intervention decisions should be made by the multidisciplinary team when symptoms remain refractory. The synopsis highlights that transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) improves symptoms and survival in selected patients with chronic severe secondary MR despite optimal GDMT and that mitral valve surgery may benefit patients with MR attributable to atrial fibrillation. The supportive text summarizes COAPT and MITRA-FR trial findings, enrollment criteria, and remodeling outcomes that inform patient selection for TEER.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for Secondary MR

rows.recommendation: In patients with chronic severe secondary MR related to LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF <50%) who have persistent symptoms (NYHA class II, III, or IV) while on optimal GDMT for HF (Stage D), TEER is reasonable in patients with appropriate anatomy as defined on TEE and with LVEF between 20% and 50%, LVESD ≤70 mm, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure ≤70 mm Hg (1–8).
In patients with severe secondary MR (Stages C and D), mitral valve surgery is reasonable when CABG is undertaken for the treatment of myocardial ischemia (9–15).

In patients with chronic severe secondary MR from atrial annular dilation with preserved LV systolic function (LVEF ≥50%) who have severe persistent symptoms (NYHA class III or IV) despite therapy for HF and therapy for associated AF or other comorbidities (Stage D), mitral valve surgery may be considered (16–20).

In patients with chronic severe secondary MR related to LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF <50%) who have persistent severe symptoms (NYHA class III or IV) while on optimal GDMT for HF (Stage D), mitral valve surgery may be considered (9,12,21–43).

In patients with CAD and chronic severe secondary MR related to LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF <50%) (Stage D) who are undergoing mitral valve surgery because of severe symptoms (NYHA class III or IV) that persist despite GDMT for HF, chordal-sparing mitral valve replacement may be reasonable to choose over downsized annuloplasty repair (9,12,21–32,44–47).

content.narrative_summary: Paragraphs 2 and 3 continue the discussion of secondary mitral regurgitation management. It states that surgical correction of chronic secondary MR has not been proven to prolong life, but observational data and a substudy of the STICH trial support addressing the mitral valve at the time of CABG in patients with severe coronary artery disease and severe MR. Secondary MR can also develop in patients with preserved LV function due to progressive left atrial dilation, leading to annular enlargement and leaflet malcoaptation.

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
content.narrative_summary: This page transitions from discussion of mitral valve surgery to the section on tricuspid valve disease. It introduces the classification and stages of tricuspid regurgitation (TR), noting that trace to mild degrees of TR are often detected on transthoracic echocardiography in anatomically normal valves, while significant or worsening TR is associated with poor long-term outcomes. The narrative describes primary causes of TR (rheumatic disease; infective endocarditis; iatrogenic factors such as device leads and endomyocardial biopsy; congenital anomalies including Ebstein’s and levo‐transposition; and other etiologies such as trauma, carcinoid, drugs, and irradiation) and secondary causes (pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular remodeling; dilated cardiomyopathy; annular dilation associated with atrial fibrillation; and right ventricular volume overload from shunts or high output). A footnote defines isolated TR. The text then outlines clinical stages C and D of severe TR, with Stage C asymptomatic patients presenting elevated central venous pressure and imaging evidence of significant TR, and Stage D symptomatic patients exhibiting fatigue, abdominal bloating, peripheral edema, and end‐organ damage. The severity of TR is noted to be dynamic and dependent on preload and pulmonary pressure.

Secondary: pulmonary hypertension with RV remodeling (primary or secondary to left‐sided heart disease); dilated cardiomyopathy; annular dilation associated with AF; RV volume overload (shunts/high output). Footnote defines isolated TR (associated with AF, LVEF >60%, pulmonary artery systolic pressure <50 mm Hg, no left‐sided valve disease).

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) can determine the etiology of tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and assess its impact on the right ventricle, with cardiac catheterization providing additional value when TTE data are inadequate or discordant. The recommendation-specific supportive text describes how TTE distinguishes primary from secondary TR, evaluates associated left-sided valvular or myocardial disease, and estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure. It also outlines parameters for RV systolic function—tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, annular velocity, end-systolic area, and fractional area change—and notes that modalities such as 3D TEE, magnetic resonance imaging, and CT may offer more accurate RV assessment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnosis of TR

rows.recommendation: In patients with TR, TTE is indicated to evaluate the presence and severity of TR, determine the etiology, measure the sizes of the right-sided chambers and inferior vena cava, assess RV systolic function, estimate pulmonary artery systolic pressure, and characterize any associated left-sided heart disease (1,2).

In patients with TR, invasive measurement of the cardiac index, right-sided diastolic pressures, pulmonary artery pressures, and pulmonary vascular resistance, as well as right ventriculography, can be useful when clinical and noninvasive data are discordant or inadequate (3–5).

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Stages of TR
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Stage B (Progressive TR): central jet <50% RA, vena contracta <0.7 cm, ERO <0.40 cm², regurgitant volume <45 mL; no hemodynamic consequences or clinical symptoms. Stage C (Asymptomatic severe TR): central jet ≥50% RA, vena contracta ≥0.7 cm, ERO ≥0.40 cm², regurgitant volume ≥45 mL, dense triangular continuous-wave signal, hepatic vein systolic flow reversal; dilated RV and RA, elevated RA c-V wave; elevated venous pressure without symptoms. Stage D (Symptomatic severe TR): same hemodynamics as Stage C; dilated RV and RA, elevated RA c-V wave; elevated venous pressure with dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, ascites, edema.

section_headings: Recommendations for Medical Therapy for TR
content.narrative_summary: This page discusses the need for invasive pulmonary artery pressure measurements when noninvasive assessments are discordant or inadequate, including the roles of right atrial pressure measurements, right ventriculography, and thermodilution cardiac output in evaluating TR and pulmonary vascular resistance. It then outlines medical therapy for tricuspid regurgitation, focusing on diuretic therapy, dietary sodium restriction, support stockings, and aldosterone antagonists in severe TR, as well as the limited role of pulmonary vasodilators and guideline‐directed medical therapy for secondary TR.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy for TR

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with signs and symptoms of right-sided HF attributable to severe TR (Stages C and D), diuretics can be useful.

section_headings: 11.1.2. Selection of Prosthetic Valve Type: Bioprosthetic Versus Mechanical Valve
content.narrative_summary: Prosthetic valve dysfunction may remain asymptomatic until hemodynamic consequences or AF develop. TTE diagnosis in asymptomatic patients can prompt timely follow-up. Standardized definitions and grading systems for structural valve deterioration of surgical and transcatheter aortic valves have been proposed. In patients with mechanical prostheses, routine annual TTE may be unnecessary if the postoperative baseline is normal and no clinical change is apparent. Durability data for bioprosthetic TAVI valves are less robust than those for surgically implanted bioprostheses; intermediate-term TAVI durability appears favorable but largely reflects observations in older patients. TAVI protocols typically include routine TTE before discharge, at 30 days, and at 1 year, with annual TTE thereafter if no clinical change.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Prosthetic Valve Type: Bioprosthetic Versus Mechanical Valve

rows.recommendation: For patients who require heart valve replacement, the choice of prosthetic valve should be based on a shared decision-making process that accounts for the patient’s values and preferences and includes discussion of the indications for and risks of anticoagulant therapy and the potential need for and risks associated with valve reintervention.
For patients of any age requiring valve replacement for whom anticoagulant therapy is contraindicated, cannot be managed appropriately, or is not desired, a bioprosthetic valve is recommended.
For patients <50 years of age who do not have a contraindication to anticoagulation and require AVR, it is reasonable to choose a mechanical aortic prosthesis over a bioprosthetic valve (1).

For patients 50 to 65 years of age who require AVR and who do not have a contraindication to anticoagulation, it is reasonable to individualize the choice of either a mechanical or bioprosthetic AVR, with consideration of individual patient factors and after informed shared decision-making (1–10).
In patients >65 years of age who require AVR, it is reasonable to choose a bioprosthesis over a mechanical valve (1).

For patients <65 years of age who have an indication for mitral valve replacement, do not have a contraindication to anticoagulation, and are unable to undergo mitral valve repair, it is reasonable to choose a mechanical mitral prosthesis over a bioprosthetic valve (1,7,10,11).
For patients ≥65 years of age who require mitral valve replacement and are unable to undergo mitral valve repair, it is reasonable to choose a bioprosthesis over a mechanical valve (1,7,11).

In patients <50 years of age who prefer a bioprosthetic AVR and have appropriate anatomy, replacement of the aortic valve by a pulmonic autograft (the Ross procedure) may be considered at a Comprehensive Valve Center (12–14).

content.title: Selected Factors That May Impact Shared Decision-Making for the Choice of Prosthetic Valve
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis describes how shared decision-making for prosthetic valve choice is influenced by patient age, values, preferences, expected bioprosthetic durability, risks of patient-prosthesis mismatch and reinvention timing, and long-term anticoagulation risks after mechanical valve replacement. Younger patients often avoid mechanical valves due to the inconvenience of lifelong VKA therapy, whereas mechanical replacement may be preferred for those at very high reoperation risk. The introduction of TAVI has altered trade-offs between mechanical and bioprosthetic options in younger patients. In the Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text, valve choice is advised based on durability, hemodynamics, risk, need for anticoagulation, and patient preferences; VKA is necessary for mechanical valves to prevent thrombosis, with no proven safety of newer anticoagulants in this setting; and patients under 50 at AVR face higher and earlier bioprosthetic deterioration with 15-year reoperation risks of 22%, 30%, and 50% at ages 50, 40, and 20 respectively, highlighting the need to balance risks (text cuts off mid-sentence).

content.title: 11.2. Antithrombotic Therapy
content.narrative_summary: The page presents recommendations for antithrombotic therapy for prosthetic heart valves. Referenced studies supporting these recommendations are summarized in Online Data Supplement 36.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antithrombotic Therapy for Prosthetic Valves

rows.recommendation: In patients with a mechanical prosthetic valve, anticoagulation with a VKA is recommended (1–5).

For patients with a mechanical bileaflet or current-generation single-tilting disk AVR and no risk factors for thromboembolism, anticoagulation with a VKA to achieve an INR of 2.5 is recommended (6–8).

For patients with a mechanical AVR and additional risk factors for thromboembolism (eg, AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable state) or an older-generation prosthesis (eg, ball-in-cage), anticoagulation with a VKA is indicated to achieve an INR of 3.0 (9,10).
For patients with a mechanical mitral valve replacement, anticoagulation with a VKA is indicated to achieve an INR of 3.0 (9,11).
For patients with a bioprosthetic TAVI, aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily is reasonable in the absence of other indications for oral anticoagulants (12–14).
For all patients with a bioprosthetic SAVR or mitral valve replacement, aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily is reasonable in the absence of other indications for oral anticoagulants (9,15–18).

For patients with a bioprosthetic SAVR or mitral valve replacement who are at low risk of bleeding, anticoagulation with a VKA to achieve an INR of 2.5 is reasonable for at least 3 months and for as long as 6 months after surgical replacement (15,19–25).

For patients with a mechanical SAVR or mitral valve replacement who are managed with a VKA and have an indication for antiplatelet therapy, addition of aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily may be considered when the risk of bleeding is low (26).

For patients with a mechanical On-X AVR and no thromboembolic risk factors, use of a VKA targeted to a lower INR (1.5–2.0) may be reasonable starting ≥3 months after surgery, with continuation of aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily (27,28).

For patients with a bioprosthetic TAVI who are at low risk of bleeding, dual-antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 75 to 100 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg may be reasonable for 3 to 6 months after valve implantation (12,13,29).

For patients with a bioprosthetic TAVI who are at low risk of bleeding, anticoagulation with a VKA to achieve an INR of 2.5 may be reasonable for at least 3 months after valve implantation (23,31–33).
For patients with bioprosthetic TAVI, treatment with low-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) plus aspirin (75–100 mg) is contraindicated in the absence of other indications for oral anticoagulants (30).
For patients with a mechanical valve prosthesis, anticoagulation with the direct thrombin inhibitor, dabigatran, is contraindicated (4,5).
For patients with a mechanical valve prosthesis, the use of anti-Xa direct oral anticoagulants has not been assessed and is not recommended (34–37).

The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes evidence supporting lifelong VKA therapy in mechanical valve patients, appropriate INR target ranges to balance thrombosis and bleeding, observational and randomized study findings on INR thresholds in different valve types and generations, and prior antiplatelet protocols after TAVI; paragraph 5 ends mid-sentence.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Bridging Therapy During Interruption of Oral Anticoagulation in Patients With Prosthetic Heart Valves

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with mechanical heart valves who are undergoing minor procedures (eg, dental extractions or cataract removal) where bleeding is easily controlled, continuation of VKA anticoagulation with a therapeutic INR is recommended.

2. For patients with a bileaflet mechanical AVR and no other risk factors for thromboembolism who are undergoing invasive procedures, temporary interruption of VKA anticoagulation, without bridging agents while the INR is subtherapeutic, is recommended.

3. For patients with a mechanical valve prosthesis receiving VKA therapy who require immediate/emergency noncardiac surgery or an invasive procedure, administration of 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (or its activated form) is reasonable.

4. For patients with bioprosthetic heart valves or annuloplasty rings who are receiving anticoagulation for AF, it is reasonable to consider the need for bridging anticoagulant therapy around the time of invasive procedures on the basis of the CHA2DS2-VASc score weighed against the risk of bleeding.

5. For patients who are undergoing invasive procedures and have 1) a mechanical AVR and any thromboembolic risk factor, 2) an older-generation mechanical AVR, or 3) a mechanical mitral valve replacement, bridging anticoagulation therapy during the preoperative time interval when the INR is subtherapeutic is reasonable on an individualized basis, with the risks of bleeding weighed against the benefits of thromboembolism prevention.

section_headings: 11.4. Excessive Anticoagulation and Serious Bleeding With Prosthetic Valves
content.narrative_summary: Points 2–5 summarize management of VKA interruption and reversal in patients with prosthetic valves: low‐risk bileaflet mechanical AVR patients may safely stop VKA 2–4 days before surgery without bridging and restart 24 hours postprocedure; emergency surgery on mechanical valves can be managed with IV prothrombin complex concentrate (onset 5–15 min, duration 12–24 h; FFP slower on onset and shorter duration) and vitamin K; some bioprosthetic and annuloplasty‐ring patients may receive DOACs guided by CHA₂DS₂‐VASc score and managed analogously to AF for bridging needs; and planned VKA interruption with UFH/LMWH bridging (INR threshold 2.0–2.5) entails specific timing without clear RCT evidence, requiring individualized decisions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Excessive Anticoagulation and Serious Bleeding in Patients With Prosthetic Valves. Referenced studies that support the recommendations are summarized in Online Data Supplement 37.

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with mechanical valves and uncontrollable bleeding who require immediate reversal of anticoagulation, administration of 4-factor prothrombin complex (or its activated form) is reasonable.

2. For patients with mechanical valves and uncontrollable bleeding who have received 4-factor prothrombin concentrate complex, adjunctive use of intravenous vitamin K is reasonable if resumption of VKA therapy is not anticipated for 7 days.

3. For patients with bioprosthetic valves or annuloplasty rings who are receiving a direct oral anticoagulant and who require immediate reversal of anticoagulation because of uncontrollable bleeding, treatment with idarucizumab (for dabigatran) or andexanet alfa (for anti-Xa agents) is reasonable.

4. For patients with a mechanical prosthetic valve and supratherapeutic INR (>5.0) who are not actively bleeding, the benefit of individualized treatment with oral vitamin K, in addition to temporary withdrawal of the VKA, is uncertain.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Thromboembolic Events With Prosthetic Valves

rows.recommendation: In patients with a mechanical AVR who experience a stroke or systemic embolic event while in therapeutic range on VKA anticoagulation, it is reasonable to increase the INR goal from 2.5 (range, 2.0–3.0) to 3.0 (range, 2.5–3.5) or to add daily low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg), with assessment of bleeding risk.

In patients with a mechanical mitral valve replacement who experience a stroke or systemic embolic event while in therapeutic range on VKA anticoagulation, it is reasonable to increase the INR goal from 3.0 (range, 2.5–3.5) to 4.0 (range, 3.5–4.0) or to add daily low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg), with assessment of bleeding risk.

In patients with a bioprosthetic surgical or transcatheter aortic valve or bioprosthetic mitral valve who experience a stroke or systemic embolic event while on antiplatelet therapy, VKA anticoagulation, instead of antiplatelet therapy may be considered after assessment of bleeding risk (1,2).

section_headings: 11.6.1. Diagnosis of Acute Mechanical Valve Thrombosis
content.narrative_summary: Mechanical valve thrombosis is typically a subacute to acute event resulting from abnormal or absent leaflet motion, often due to inadequate anticoagulation. Patients may present with a stenotic murmur, muffled closing clicks, or acute pulmonary edema. Urgent imaging (TTE, TEE, fluoroscopy, or CT) assesses valve function, leaflet motion, and thrombus. In thrombosed mechanical valves, prompt therapy—either slow-infusion, low-dose fibrinolytic therapy or emergency surgery—is recommended, with decisions individualized by the heart valve team based on clinical factors and local expertise.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of prosthetic valve evaluation, noting that cine-CT 3D imaging is less operator dependent than fluoroscopy and permits detection of pannus or thrombus on or adjacent to the valve. It highlights increased identification of subclinical bioprosthetic valve thrombosis with CT imaging of transcatheter valves (3–7) and suggests 3D TEE or 4D CT may detect thrombus causing obstruction. Section 11.8.2 introduces intervention recommendations. The 'Synopsis' describes higher cumulative survival with reoperative AVR versus transcatheter ViV in 459 patients (40% isolated stenosis, 30% mixed lesions), reports 1-month mortality of 7.6%, overall 1-year survival 83.2%, 93% with NYHA I/II at follow-up, and notes similar hemodynamics but lower stroke/bleeding with ViV (15). A subset with leaflet thrombosis may respond to anticoagulation (Figure 14) (6–13). The page ends in the middle of the 'Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text'.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for Prosthetic Valve Stenosis

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with symptomatic severe stenosis of a bioprosthetic or mechanical prosthetic valve, repeat surgical intervention is indicated unless surgical risk is high or prohibitive (1–3).

2. For severely symptomatic patients with bioprosthetic aortic valve stenosis and high or prohibitive surgical risk, a transcatheter ViV procedure is reasonable when performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (4,5).
3. For patients with significant bioprosthetic valve stenosis attributable to suspected or documented valve thrombosis, oral anticoagulation with a VKA is reasonable (6–13).

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of leaflet thrombosis in prosthetic valves, noting that leaflet thrombosis may occur from 1 month to years after implantation and that stable patients without contraindications may be managed with a trial of oral anticoagulation with VKA, but require close follow-up due to risk of recurrent thrombosis and structural deterioration. Section 11.9 then defines prosthetic valve regurgitation: in mechanical valves it may be transvalvular (disk motion impairment from pannus, thrombus, vegetation) or paravalvular (suture line disruption, technical error, endocarditis), and in bioprosthetic valves it is often transvalvular (leaflet immobility from calcification or perforation), with echocardiographic severity definitions published by ASE.

content.title: 11.9.1. Diagnosis of Prosthetic Valve Regurgitation
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses the variable clinical presentation of prosthetic valve regurgitation, including incidental detection in asymptomatic patients and symptomatic presentations with heart failure or hemolysis. It notes limitations of TTE for prosthetic mitral valves and the necessity of TEE to distinguish transvalvular from paravalvular leaks. The recommendation-specific supportive text emphasizes echocardiography as the primary imaging modality, acoustic shadowing issues affecting TTE and TEE, the VARC grading scheme for paravalvular leak severity, and the role of 3D echocardiography in precise leak assessment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnosis of Prosthetic Valve Regurgitation

rows.recommendation: In patients with suspected mechanical or bioprosthetic valve regurgitation, TTE and TEE are recommended to determine the cause and severity of the leak, assess ventricular function, and estimate pulmonary artery systolic pressure (1–4).
In patients undergoing a transcatheter procedure for paravalvular prosthetic regurgitation, 3D TEE is recommended for intraprocedural guidance (4–7).

content.title: 11.9.3. Intervention
content.narrative_summary: Prosthetic valve degeneration leads to regurgitation from leaflet calcification, noncoaptation, or leaflet tear/perforation, causing acute or chronic heart failure symptoms. Paravalvular leak can cause hemolysis and anemia; infection must be excluded before intervention. Symptomatic patients with paravalvular leak are best managed by surgery, with percutaneous closure reasonable if surgical risk is high or prohibitive. Bioprosthetic valve regurgitation may be managed surgically or with a transcatheter valve-in-valve (ViV) procedure in high-risk patients. Rapid progression of bioprosthetic regurgitation may warrant re-replacement even in asymptomatic patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention

rows.recommendation: In patients with intractable hemolysis or HF attributable to prosthetic transvalvular or paravalvular leak, surgery is recommended unless surgical risk is high or prohibitive (1–4).
In asymptomatic patients with severe prosthetic regurgitation and low operative risk, surgery is reasonable (1–4).

In patients with prosthetic paravalvular regurgitation with the following: 1) either intractable hemolysis or NYHA class III or IV symptoms and 2) who are at high or prohibitive surgical risk and 3) have anatomic features suitable for catheter-based therapy, percutaneous repair of paravalvular leak is reasonable when performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (5–9).

For patients with severe HF symptoms caused by bioprosthetic valve regurgitation who are at high to prohibitive surgical risk, a transcatheter ViV procedure is reasonable when performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (10–12).

content.title: 12. INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS
content.narrative_summary: This page introduces infective endocarditis, classifying it by whether a native or prosthetic valve is affected and by timing of infection after valve intervention. It emphasizes the importance of prevention in all valve disease patients, notes evolving causative organisms with a rise in drug-use–associated cases, and reports in-hospital mortality of 15%–20% and 1-year mortality approaching 40%. Noninfective endocarditis types are excluded from these guidelines. The narrative then transitions to diagnostic recommendations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnosis of IE

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients at risk of IE (eg, those with congenital or acquired VHD, previous IE, prosthetic heart valves, certain congenital or heritable heart malformations, immunodeficiency states, or injection drug use) who have unexplained fever blood, culture samples should be obtained. (1)
2. In patients with the recent onset of left-sided valve regurgitation, at least 2 sets of blood culture samples should be obtained (1–12).
3. In patients with suspected IE, the Modified Duke Criteria should be used for diagnosis (Tables 24 and 25) (2–10).

content.title: Recommendations (Continued)
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis states that the Modified Duke Criteria are the current standard for endocarditis diagnosis, incorporating clinical, imaging, and bacteriological criteria and validated across diverse patient groups. It emphasizes obtaining blood culture results before initiating antibiotic therapy in valvular heart disease with known or suspected infective endocarditis, involving infectious disease experts on the Heart Valve multidisciplinary team, and highlights the critical role of TTE, TEE, CT, and CT/PET imaging in diagnosis. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text begins with guidance on blood culture sampling timing and its importance.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations (Continued)

rows.recommendation: 4. Patients with IE should be evaluated and managed with consultation with a multispecialty Heart Valve Team, which includes an infectious disease specialist, cardiologist, and cardiac surgeon; a cardiac anesthesiologist for surgically managed patients (11); and a neurologist for patients with neurological events (11–13).

5. In patients with suspected IE, TTE is recommended to identify vegetations, characterize the hemodynamic severity of valvular lesions, assess ventricular function and pulmonary pressures, and detect complications (14–23).

6. In all patients with known or suspected IE and nondiagnostic TTE results, when complications have developed or are clinically suspected or when intracardiac device leads are present, TEE is recommended (21,23–40).

7. In patients with IE who have a change in clinical signs or symptoms (eg, new murmur, embolism, persistent fever, HF, abscess, or atrioventricular heart block) and in patients at high risk of complications (eg, extensive infected tissue, large vegetation on initial echocardiogram, or staphylococcal, enterococcal, or fungal infections), TTE and/or TEE are recommended for reevaluation (24,31,41–46).
8. In patients undergoing valve surgery for IE, intraoperative TEE is recommended (47–50).

9. In patients being considered for an early change to oral antibiotic therapy for the treatment of stable IE, a baseline TEE before switching to oral therapy and a repeat TEE 1 to 3 days before completion of the oral antibiotic regimen should be performed (51).
10. In patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia without a known source, TEE is reasonable to diagnose possible IE (11,36,52–56).
11. In patients with a prosthetic valve in the presence of persistent fever without bacteremia or a new murmur, a TEE is reasonable to aid in the diagnosis of IE (57–60).
12. In patients in whom the anatomy cannot be clearly delineated by echocardiography in the setting of suspected paravalvular infections, CT imaging is reasonable (37,61–68).
13. In patients classified by Modified Duke Criteria as having “possible IE,” 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT is reasonable as adjunct diagnostic imaging (69–71).
14. In patients with nosocomial S. aureus bacteremia with a known portal of entry from an extracardiac source, TEE might be considered to detect concomitant staphylococcal IE (22,53,54,72–74).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy for IE

rows.recommendation: In patients with IE, appropriate antibiotic therapy should be initiated and continued after blood cultures are obtained, with guidance from antibiotic sensitivity data and the infectious disease experts on the MDT (1–7).
Patients with suspected or confirmed IE associated with drug use should be referred to addiction treatment for opioid substitution therapy (8–10).

content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis outlines that specific antimicrobial regimens from prior AHA, European, and British guidelines are not repeated, highlights risks of continued anticoagulation in AF or mechanical valves, management of intravenous drug users including referral to addiction programs, criteria for conversion from IV to oral antibiotics guided by TEE, and the frequent need (≈50%) for early surgical intervention (Figure 15). rows.recommendation: 3. In patients with IE and with evidence of cerebral embolism or stroke, regardless of the other indications for anticoagulation, it is reasonable to temporarily discontinue anticoagulation (11–24).

4. In patients with left-sided IE caused by streptococcus, Enterococcus faecalis, S. aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococci deemed stable by the MDT after initial intravenous antibiotics, a change to oral antibiotic therapy may be considered if TEE before the switch to oral therapy shows no paravalvular infection, if frequent and appropriate follow-up can be assured by the care team, and if a follow-up TEE can be performed 1 to 3 days before the completion of the antibiotic course. (25)
5. In patients receiving VKA anticoagulation at the time of IE diagnosis, temporary discontinuation of VKA anticoagulation may be considered (13,26–34).
6. Patients with known VHD should not receive antibiotics before blood cultures are obtained for unexplained fever (22,35,36).

content.title: Recommendations for Intervention for IE
content.narrative_summary: Continued discussion of management considerations in infective endocarditis, including anticoagulation use with VKA and UFH, and recommendations for obtaining minimum blood cultures for microbiological diagnosis.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for IE

rows.recommendation: Decisions about the timing of surgical intervention for IE should be made by a Heart Valve Team (1–6).

In patients with IE who present with valve dysfunction resulting in symptoms of HF, early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) is indicated (7–19).

In patients with left-sided IE caused by S. aureus, a fungal organism, or other highly resistant organisms, early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) is indicated (7,9,15,20–35).

In patients with IE complicated by heart block, annular or aortic abscess, or destructive penetrating lesions, early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) is indicated (7,9,36–44).

In patients with IE and evidence of persistent infection as manifested by persistent bacteremia or fevers lasting >5 days after onset of appropriate antimicrobial therapy, early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) for IE is indicated (7,9,15,25,26,45–48).

In all patients with definite endocarditis and an implanted cardiac electronic device, complete removal of the pacemaker or defibrillator systems, including all leads and the generator, is indicated (49–55).

For patients with prosthetic valve endocarditis and relapsing infection (defined as recurrence of bacteremia after a complete course of appropriate antibiotics and subsequent negative blood culture results) without other identifiable source of infection, surgery is recommended (7).

The Synopsis describes that management requires a Heart Valve multidisciplinary team including infectious disease and neurology, notes indications for early surgery (HF, persistent infection, abscess, heart block, resistant organisms, recurrent emboli), and that device-related infections mandate system removal. Cerebral embolic events are not contraindications to surgery unless there is extensive neurological damage or intracranial hemorrhage. In patients with recurrent endocarditis and continued intravenous drug use, consultation with addiction medicine is recommended to discuss the long-term prognosis for the patient's refraining from actions that risk reinfection before repeat surgical intervention is considered (56–60).

9. In patients with IE who present with recurrent emboli and persistent vegetations despite appropriate antibiotic therapy, early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) is reasonable (53,61–66).

10. In patients with native left-sided valve endocarditis who exhibit mobile vegetations >10 mm in length (with or without clinical evidence of embolic phenomenon), early surgery (during initial hospitalization and before completion of a full therapeutic course of antibiotics) may be considered (20,61–63,67).

11. In patients with IE and an indication for surgery who have suffered a stroke but have no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage or extensive neurological damage, operation without delay may be considered (68–70).

12. For patients with IE and major ischemic stroke with extensive neurological damage or intracranial hemorrhage, if the patient is hemodynamically stable, delaying valve surgery for at least 4 weeks may be considered (68,71).

content.title: 13. PREGNANCY AND VHD
section_headings: 13.1. Initial Management of Women With VHD Before and During Pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: This section introduces the hemodynamic changes of pregnancy, noting these are usually well tolerated in structurally normal hearts but pose challenges in women with valvular heart disease (VHD). The synopsis emphasizes comprehensive preconception evaluation and individualized follow-up during pregnancy based on lesion type and severity. The supportive text details risks to mother and fetus, the role of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), counseling by experienced cardiologists, assessment of functional capacity and valve lesions, discussion of medication risks, and management options before and during pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Initial Management of Women With VHD Before and During Pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Women with suspected valve disease who are considering pregnancy should undergo a clinical evaluation and TTE before pregnancy (1–5).

Women with severe valve disease (Stages C and D) who are considering pregnancy should undergo pre-pregnancy counseling by a cardiologist with expertise in managing women with VHD during pregnancy (1–5).

Pregnant women with severe valve disease (Stages C and D) should be monitored in a tertiary-care center with a dedicated Heart Valve Team of cardiologists, surgeons, anesthesiologists, and maternal-fetal medicine obstetricians with expertise in the management of high-risk cardiac conditions during pregnancy (1–12).
In asymptomatic women with severe valve disease (Stage C1) who are considering pregnancy, exercise testing is reasonable before pregnancy for risk assessment (3–5,11,13–15).

section_headings: 13.1.1. Medical Therapy for Women With VHD Before and During Pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Women with severe valvular heart disease (VHD) are at risk of heart failure, arrhythmia, and other cardiac disorders during pregnancy. Although medical therapy may preserve maternal health, it may have negative consequences for the fetus. Data from the ROPAC registry demonstrated associations between cardiac medication use during pregnancy and adverse fetal outcomes, partly attributable to underlying maternal cardiac disease. Anticoagulation for pregnant women with atrial fibrillation should follow nonpregnant guidelines, with further discussion in section 13.2.2.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy of Pregnant Women With VHD

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with VHD, beta-blocker medications are reasonable as required for heart rate control or treatment of arrhythmias (1–6).
In pregnant women with VHD and HF symptoms (Stage D), diuretic medications are reasonable if needed for volume overload (7,8).
In pregnant women with VHD, ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be given because of fetal risk (6,9–11).
