content.title: 13.1.2.1. Pre-Pregnancy Intervention
section_headings: 13.1.2. Intervention for Women With Native VHD Before and During Pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: The page presents seven evidence-based recommendations for pre-pregnancy intervention in women with native valvular heart disease, detailing COR and LOE for each. The Synopsis summarizes indications—symptoms, valve morphology, and shared decision-making for valve choice. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text expands on standard indications, anticoagulation considerations, valve thrombosis risks, and preliminary trial data on warfarin dosing.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Pre-Pregnancy Intervention in Women With VHD

rows.recommendation: 1. In symptomatic women with severe VHD who are considering pregnancy, intervention before pregnancy is recommended on the basis of standard indications (1–11).

2. In women who require a valve intervention before pregnancy, the choice of prosthetic valve should be based on a shared decision-making process that accounts for the patient’s values and preferences, including discussion of the risks of mechanical valves during pregnancy and the reduced durability of bioprosthetic valves in young women.

3. In asymptomatic women with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm², Stage C1) who are considering pregnancy, PMBC at a Comprehensive Valve Center is reasonable before pregnancy for those who have favorable valve morphology (1–5,12,13).

4. In women of childbearing age who require valve replacement, bioprosthetic valves are preferred over mechanical valves because of the increased maternal and fetal risks of mechanical heart valves in pregnancy (14).
5. In asymptomatic women with severe AS (aortic velocity ≥4.0 m/s or mean pressure gradient ≥40 mm Hg, Stage C) who are considering pregnancy, valve intervention before pregnancy is reasonable.

6. In asymptomatic women with severe AS (aortic velocity ≥4.0 m/s or mean pressure gradient ≥40 mm Hg, Stage C1) who are considering pregnancy, do not meet COR 1 criteria for intervention, and have a pre-conception evaluation confirming the absence of symptoms (including normal exercise stress testing and serum BNP measurements), medical management during pregnancy may be considered to avoid prosthetic valve replacement.

7. In asymptomatic women with severe MR (Stage C1) and a valve suitable for repair who are considering pregnancy, valve repair before pregnancy at a Comprehensive Valve Center may be considered but only after detailed discussion with the patient about the risks and benefits of the surgery and its effect on future pregnancies.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion on management of valvular heart disease during pregnancy, noting that some women with severe asymptomatic aortic stenosis (AS) and normal left ventricular function may undergo pregnancy without valve intervention but require balancing risks of mechanical valve complications and bioprosthetic deterioration. It describes options such as percutaneous balloon dilation or surgical valve replacement, the higher threshold for intervention in asymptomatic regurgitation, and high-risk features (depressed LV function, pulmonary hypertension) that warrant referral to a Comprehensive Valve Center for individualized decision-making.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention During Pregnancy in Women With VHD

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with severe AS (mean pressure gradient ≥40 mm Hg, Stage D), valve intervention during pregnancy is reasonable if there is hemodynamic deterioration or if there are NYHA class III or IV HF symptoms (1–7).

In pregnant women with severe rheumatic MS (mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm2, Stage D) and with valve morphology favorable for PMBC who remain symptomatic with NYHA class III or IV HF symptoms despite medical therapy, PMBC is reasonable during pregnancy if it is performed at a Comprehensive Valve Center (8–12).
In pregnant women with severe valve regurgitation and with NYHA class IV HF symptoms (Stage D) refractory to medical therapy, valve surgery is reasonable during pregnancy (13–16).
In pregnant women with VHD, valve surgeries should not be performed in the absence of severe HF symptoms refractory to medical therapy (13–16).

content.title: Recommendations for Initial Management of Prosthetic Heart Valves in Pregnant Women
content.narrative_summary: Continues discussion on valvular interventions during pregnancy, noting percutaneous mitral balloon dilation is high risk and reserved for cases of hemodynamic deterioration or severe NYHA class III/IV symptoms, requiring a multidisciplinary high‐risk obstetrics team; regurgitant lesions are generally better tolerated than stenotic ones. The Synopsis highlights that pregnancy in women with mechanical heart valves is WHO Risk Category III with approximately 1% maternal mortality and a 5% valve thrombosis risk, emphasizing the need for specialized expertise. Recommendation‐Specific Supportive Text describes the use of preconception TTE to assess valve and ventricular function and counsel patients, and explains that anticoagulation during pregnancy demands tailored strategies with frequent VKA or heparin titration due to hypercoagulability and increased transvalvular gradients; a comprehensive Heart Valve Team and maternal‐fetal medicine team are required if intervention is needed.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Initial Management of Prosthetic Heart Valves in Pregnant Women

rows.recommendation: 1. Women with a prosthetic valve should undergo pre-pregnancy assessment, including echocardiography, by a cardiologist with expertise in managing women with VHD during pregnancy.

2. Pregnant women with a mechanical prosthesis should be monitored in a tertiary-care center with a dedicated MDT of cardiologists, surgeons, anesthesiologists, and maternal-fetal medicine obstetricians with expertise in the management of high-risk cardiac conditions during pregnancy (1-3).

3. Women with mechanical heart valves considering pregnancy should be counselled that pregnancy is high risk and that there is no anticoagulation strategy that is consistently safe for the mother and baby (3-6).
4. Pregnant women with a mechanical prosthetic valve who have prosthetic valve obstruction or experience an embolic event should undergo a TEE (7-9).

content.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease
section_headings: 13.2.2. Anticoagulation for Pregnant Women With Mechanical Prosthetic Heart Valves
content.narrative_summary: Counseling for women with mechanical heart valves is essential, as no anticoagulation strategy is entirely safe: maternal mortality exceeds 1% and serious maternal and fetal complications are common. Pregnancy further increases the risk of mechanical valve thrombosis, warranting high clinical suspicion in cases of embolic events, deterioration, heart failure symptoms, or increased valve gradients or regurgitation. Transesophageal echocardiography, fluoroscopy, and gated cardiac CT are useful to evaluate suspected valve thrombosis during pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Anticoagulation for Pregnant Women With Mechanical Prosthetic Heart Valves

rows.recommendation: Pregnant women with mechanical prostheses should receive therapeutic anticoagulation with frequent monitoring during pregnancy.
Women with mechanical heart valves who cannot maintain therapeutic anticoagulation with frequent monitoring should be counseled against pregnancy.

Women with mechanical heart valves and their providers should use shared decision-making to choose an anticoagulation strategy for pregnancy. Women should be informed that VKA during pregnancy is associated with the lowest likelihood of maternal complications but the highest likelihood of miscarriage, fetal death, and congenital abnormalities, particularly if taken during the first trimester and if the warfarin dose exceeds 5 mg/d.

Pregnant women with mechanical valve prostheses who are on warfarin should switch to twice-daily LMWH (with a target anti-Xa level of 0.8 U/mL to 1.2 U/mL at 4 to 6 hours after dose) or intravenous UFH (with an activated partial thromboplastin time [aPTT] 2 times control) at least 1 week before planned delivery.
Pregnant women with mechanical valve prostheses who are on LMWH should switch to UFH (with an aPTT 2 times control) at least 36 hours before planned delivery.
Pregnant women with valve prostheses should stop UFH at least 6 hours before planned vaginal delivery.
If labor begins or urgent delivery is required in a woman therapeutically anticoagulated with a VKA, cesarean section should be performed after reversal of anticoagulation.

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses who require a dose of warfarin ≤5 mg/d to maintain a therapeutic INR, continuation of warfarin for all 3 trimesters is reasonable after full discussion with the patient about risks and benefits.

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses who require >5 mg/d of warfarin to achieve a therapeutic INR, dose-adjusted LMWH (with a target anti-Xa level of 0.8 to 1.2 U/mL at 4 to 6 hours after dose) at least 2 times per day during the first trimester, followed by warfarin during the second and third trimesters, is reasonable.

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses who require a dose of warfarin >5 mg/d to achieve a therapeutic INR, and for whom dose-adjusted LMWH is unavailable, dose-adjusted continuous intravenous UFH during the first trimester (with aPTT 2 times control), followed by warfarin for the second and third trimesters, is reasonable.

content.title: Recommendations (Continued)
content.narrative_summary: Pregnant women with mechanical heart valves face high risks of maternal and fetal complications and require uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation despite trade-offs between maternal safety and fetal safety. Warfarin is most effective but crosses the placenta causing fetal harm; LMWH is not teratogenic but may increase maternal thrombosis risk if not properly dosed and monitored. Three anticoagulation strategies are outlined: continue warfarin throughout pregnancy, use heparin throughout pregnancy, or sequential therapy (heparin in the first trimester and warfarin thereafter). Supportive text emphasizes the prohibitive risk of valve failure or stroke without adequate anticoagulation, the impact of improper dosing or monitoring on maternal morbidity and mortality, and the absence of a universally safe strategy for both mother and fetus.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations (Continued)

rows.recommendation: For hemodynamically stable pregnant women with obstructive left-sided mechanical valve thrombosis, it is reasonable to manage with slow-infusion, low-dose fibrinolytic therapy (26).

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses who require a warfarin dose >5 mg/d to achieve a therapeutic INR, dose-adjusted LMWH (with a target anti-Xa level of 0.8 to 1.2 U/mL at 4 to 6 hours after dose) at least 2 times per day for all 3 trimesters may be considered (3,6,14–16,27).

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses who require a dose of warfarin ≤5 mg/d to maintain a therapeutic INR, dose-adjusted LMWH at least 2 times per day during the first trimester, followed by warfarin for the second and third trimesters, may be considered (1–3,6,12,16,22).
For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses, aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily may be considered, in addition to anticoagulation, if needed for other indications (28).

For pregnant women with mechanical prostheses, LMWH should not be administered unless anti-Xa levels are monitored 4 to 6 hours after administration and dose is adjusted according to levels (8–10,15,27).
For patients with mechanical valve prostheses, anticoagulation with the direct thrombin inhibitor, dabigatran, should not be administered (29).
The use of anti-Xa direct oral anticoagulants with mechanical heart valves in pregnancy has not been assessed and is not recommended (30–32).

14.1.1. Management of CAD in Patients Undergoing TAVI
content.narrative_summary: Continues discussion of anticoagulation in pregnant patients with mechanical heart valves. Emphasizes that low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) requires meticulous anti-factor Xa monitoring (trough >0.6 IU/mL) to maintain therapeutic anticoagulation. Notes that warfarin ≤5 mg/day reduces but does not eliminate embryopathy risk and may be substituted with LMWH in the first trimester at the cost of increased maternal thrombotic complications. States that low-dose aspirin is safe in pregnancy when indicated. Describes that fixed-dose LMWH without anti-Xa monitoring is associated with high rates of valve thrombosis and that dose-adjusted LMWH throughout pregnancy improves outcomes. Reports that dabigatran and other anti-Xa direct oral anticoagulants have not been shown to be safe in patients with mechanical heart valves and should not be used in pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of CAD in Patients Undergoing TAVI

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing TAVI, 1) contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography (in patients with a low pretest probability for CAD) or 2) an invasive coronary angiogram is recommended to assess coronary anatomy and guide revascularization.
In patients undergoing TAVI with significant left main or proximal CAD with or without angina, revascularization by PCI before TAVI is reasonable (1,2).

In patients with significant AS and significant CAD (luminal reduction >70% diameter, fractional flow reserve <0.8, instantaneous wave-free ratio <0.89) consisting of complex bifurcation left main and/or multivessel CAD with a SYNTAX (Synergy Between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention With Taxus and Cardiac Surgery) score >33, SAVR and CABG are reasonable and preferred over TAVI and PCI (3,4).

section_headings: 14.1.2. Management of CAD in Patients Undergoing Valve Surgery
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion on assessing and managing coronary artery disease (CAD) in valvular heart disease (VHD). Fractional flow reserve and instantaneous wave-free ratio are safe, feasible methods for evaluating coronary lesions in TAVI candidates; no randomized trials guide timing of PCI before TAVI, and decisions are individualized. Combining TAVI with PCI is common, though timing of pre- or post-TAVI PCI remains controversial. Surgical revascularization may benefit VHD patients with complex CAD (eg, SYNTAX score >33 or >50% stenosis). The Synopsis emphasizes that CAD and VHD often coexist, revascularization impacts procedural risk and long-term outcomes, and an aggressive approach is appropriate. Contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography is increasingly used. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text notes that CAD is prevalent in VHD, contributes to angina and risk stratification, and has lower prevalence in younger/premenopausal patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of CAD in Patients Undergoing Valve Surgery

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with symptoms of angina, objective evidence of ischemia, decreased LV systolic function, history of CAD, or coronary risk factors (including men >40 years of age and postmenopausal women), invasive coronary angiography is indicated before valve intervention (1–8).
2. In patients with chronic severe secondary MR, invasive coronary angiography should be performed as part of the evaluation (9–11).
3. In selected patients with a low to intermediate pretest probability of CAD, contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography is reasonable to exclude the presence of significant obstructive CAD (12–18).

4. In patients undergoing valve repair or replacement with significant proximal CAD (≥70% reduction in luminal diameter in major coronary arteries or ≥50% reduction in luminal diameter in the left main coronary artery and/or physiologically significance), CABG is reasonable for selective patients (19,20).

section_headings: 14.2. Intervention for AF in Patients With VHD
content.narrative_summary: Continuation of a numbered list of preoperative considerations for patients undergoing valve surgery, including the absence of atherosclerotic risk factors or mediastinal radiation; the evaluation of functional mitral regurgitation due to left ventricular dysfunction and the need to assess coronary anatomy; the use of contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography in selected low- to intermediate-risk patients prior to transcatheter or surgical intervention; and the recommendation to perform concomitant coronary artery bypass grafting when uncorrected coronary artery disease is present because it improves perioperative and late outcomes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Intervention for AF in Patients With VHD

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with VHD and AF for whom surgical intervention is planned, the potential symptomatic benefits and additional procedural risks of adjunctive arrhythmia surgery at the time of cardiac valvular surgery should be discussed with the patient (1–11).

2. For symptomatic patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF who are undergoing valvular surgery, surgical pulmonary vein isolation or a maze procedure can be beneficial to reduce symptoms and prevent recurrent arrhythmias (1,2,12–15).
3. For patients with AF or atrial flutter who are undergoing valve surgery, LA appendage ligation/excision is reasonable to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events (16–19).
4. In patients undergoing LA surgical ablation of atrial arrhythmias and/or LA appendage ligation/excision, anticoagulation therapy is reasonable for at least 3 months after the procedure (20–22).
5. For patients without atrial arrhythmias who are undergoing valvular surgery, LA appendage occlusion/exclusion/amputation is potentially harmful (23).

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis indicates that for patients undergoing valve surgery with symptomatic atrial fibrillation (AF) or atrial flutter, a concomitant maze procedure with or without left atrial appendage occlusion/exclusion effectively treats the arrhythmia but requires postoperative anticoagulation for at least 3 months. The supportive text reviews multiple studies demonstrating that surgical ablations—pulmonary vein isolation and modified left, right, or biatrial maze procedures—at the time of valvular surgery reduce AF recurrence but increase operative time, procedural complications, and the likelihood of permanent pacemaker implantation. It also notes the lack of large randomized data on mortality and stroke outcomes, clarifies that the ‘‘maze’’ refers specifically to a biatrial lesion set via cut-and-sew or energy ablation techniques, and highlights that combined mitral valve surgery with atrial maze yields greater freedom from recurrent AF.

content.narrative_summary: Echocardiographic evaluation should be performed within 12 months if there is no clinical change to quantify valve stenosis or regurgitation, assess systolic and diastolic function, chamber sizes, and estimate pulmonary artery pressure. content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: In asymptomatic patients with significant valvular heart disease (VHD) who do not meet standard criteria for intervention, the risk of noncardiac surgery can be minimized by selecting an appropriate anesthetic approach tailored to the valve lesion, ensuring intra- and perioperative hemodynamic monitoring, and optimizing loading conditions while accounting for comorbidities such as LV and RV dysfunction, coronary artery disease (CAD), pulmonary hypertension, and severity of aortic stenosis (AS). content.narrative_summary: This section emphasizes the need for improved measures of myocardial performance (beyond simple LV dimensions) and earlier detection of myocardial dysfunction using novel imaging and biomarkers. It highlights underrepresentation of older adults, women, and minorities in trials, and the need for RCTs and registries addressing asymptomatic severe valvular disease (AS, AR, MR, TR) and long-term outcomes of valve repair or replacement. Section 16.4 discusses balancing native valve disease outcomes with durability of repair/replacement, the promise of transcatheter valve therapies, and the unknown long-term durability beyond five years. In patients requiring mechanical valves, effective low-risk oral anticoagulation is needed. Moderate to severe valvular heart disease (VHD) affects 2.5% of the US population, increasing with age; many require intervention yet face high adverse outcome risk. Urgent research is called for on VHD therapies, including national/international registries, RCTs, continuous outcome evaluations at specialized centers, and patient-centric decision-making with accessible quality data.
